summary: Comments on proposals to extend TCP, arguing that the backward-compatible extensions in RFC 1072 and RFC 1185 should not be pursued, and proposing another way to evolve the protocol suite. It is informational.

eli5.summary: The author says that patching an old toy again and again is a bad idea, and suggests a different path.

questions: why were tcp extensions considered harmful
should you extend old protocols or create new ones
how do you deploy new protocol versions
subtitle: An argument for protocol evolution over backward-compatible extensions to TCP.

tldr.problem: TCP needs improvements to work well on high-capacity networks, but proposed backward-compatible extensions in RFCs 1072 and 1185 add complexity and fragility rather than solving problems cleanly.
tldr.mechanism: Instead of backward-compatible extensions, the RFC proposes maintaining multiple versions of TCP and selecting the right version for each connection using a version control layer called VTCP.
tldr.outcome: The RFC argues that protocol evolution—keeping old versions alive alongside new ones—is simpler and more maintainable than trying to extend old protocols indefinitely.

facts.label: Authors
facts.value: Stephen O'Malley and Larry L. Peterson

facts.label: RFCs criticized
facts.value: RFC 1072 (TCP Extensions), RFC 1185 (TCP Window and Sequence Number Scaling)

today: RFC 1263 is an Informational RFC expressing a research team's position on protocol design. The protocol evolution approach advocated here influenced later thinking about protocol versioning. While TCP itself has been extended rather than evolved wholesale, modern protocols often support multiple versions or use version negotiation, reflecting some of the principles this RFC articulated.

sections.title: The Problem: TCP Has Hit Its Limits
sections.content:
By 1991, the Internet was becoming much faster, but TCP had fundamental limits. The maximum TCP window size (16 bits, allowing at most 64 kilobytes in flight) is too small for high-speed, high-latency networks. Additionally, TCP sequence numbers wrap around too quickly on fast links, risking confusion between old and new packets. The RFC notes that at least eight separate changes to TCP have been proposed, raising the question of how best to evolve the protocol without breaking the Internet.

RFC 1072 and RFC 1185 proposed backward-compatible extensions: adding options to the TCP header to carry timestamps and window scaling factors, so old and new TCP versions could talk to each other. However, this approach adds complexity, creates implementation pitfalls, and leaves the protocol with vestigial code for features that are rarely used.
sections.eli5: Imagine a car designed to go 60 miles per hour on old roads. Now there are highways where cars need to go 150 mph. You could add a complicated upgrade that sometimes works with old cars, or you could design a new, faster car.

sections.title: Three Ways to Evolve a Protocol
sections.content:
The RFC compares three approaches to protocol change. Protocol creation means designing a completely new protocol, which gives freedom but at high cost and risk. Backward-compatible extensions mean modifying the old protocol so new and old versions work together—cheap to deploy but complex, fragile, and slower to distribute across the Internet. Protocol evolution means making clean changes to the protocol without worrying about old versions, then running multiple versions in parallel until the old one dies out naturally.

The RFC argues that each approach has its place: creation for entirely new functionality, extensions for behavior changes that do not affect the header, and evolution for changes to header fields or when algorithms are replaced. When combined, the three approaches let the Internet improve without being stuck maintaining compatibility forever.
sections.eli5: You can make a completely new toy (expensive), patch the old toy so it works with the new one (confusing), or keep making improved versions of the toy side by side (cleanest).

sections.title: How Protocol Evolution Would Work
sections.content:
The RFC proposes a version control layer called VTCP that sits between applications and TCP. When a connection is made, VTCP checks which version of TCP both machines support and automatically uses the highest common version. This allows running TCP[0] (classic TCP) alongside TCP[1] (an improved version for high-speed networks) on the same machine. No application needs to change; VTCP handles the selection transparently.

Each TCP version is assigned a unique identifier. The RFC proposes expanding IP's protocol number field from 8 to 32 bits and moving it to the end of the IP header, which allows dozens of TCP variants without exhausting the protocol number space. VTCP could learn which versions a machine supports by caching past connections or by querying the machine the first time—a small UDP packet asking "which TCP versions do you support?" The cache allows VTCP to avoid the query cost on subsequent connections.
sections.eli5: A smart dispatcher (VTCP) watches connections and picks the right version of TCP for each one—the new fast one if both computers support it, the old one if not. The computer remembers what works, so it does not have to ask every time.

sections.title: Applying Evolution to TCP's Needs
sections.content:
The RFC examines the specific TCP improvements proposed in RFCs 1072 and 1185. For round-trip timing, RFC 1072 proposes an ECHO option to carry timestamps in every packet. Using protocol evolution, TCP[1] simply adds 32-bit echo and echo-reply fields to the header itself, simplifying the code and avoiding the complexity of optional fields that old TCP might misunderstand.

For window size and sequence number space, RFC 1072's window-scaling option and RFC 1185's timestamp-based duplicate detection add complicated logic. Using evolution, TCP[1] can simply increase the window field from 16 to 32 bits and the sequence number field from 32 to 64 bits—trivial changes that require no complex algorithms, no dependence on accurate system clocks, and no risk of two duplicate-detection schemes interfering with each other. On modern RISC processors that support 64-bit arithmetic, this is the right choice.
sections.eli5: Instead of adding complicated patches that try to work with old TCP, just add bigger number fields to the header. It is simpler and works correctly.

sections.title: How New Versions Get Deployed
sections.content:
The RFC acknowledges that distributing new protocol versions requires infrastructure, but argues it is tractable. In the short term, a new version can be distributed as informally as a backward-compatible extension. In the medium term, the IAB could approve new TCP versions annually, with simple software distribution mechanisms (like Unix RDIST or Mach SUP) copying new versions to machines. High-performance systems have natural incentive to update—they need the new TCP to drive high-capacity networks.

Older machines too slow for high-speed networks can be ignored; there is no requirement to update them. The RFC suggests that in the long term, protocols could be designed application-by-application without central standardization, deployed through a protocol "backplane" that installs protocols automatically. Crucially, old protocol versions never disappear from the network—they simply work as well as they ever did, eliminating any risk of breaking things.
sections.eli5: Fast computers on fast networks will want the new, fast TCP, so they will update automatically. Slow computers can keep the old TCP forever and still work fine. No rush, no disruption.

left.title: Backward-compatible extension
left.desc: Old and new versions must talk directly. Requires optional fields and complex negotiation. Fragile.

right.title: Protocol evolution
right.desc: Multiple clean versions coexist. A dispatcher (VTCP) picks the right one per connection. Simple and reliable.
